summary.text: Choose a prime \(p\ge \max(N,55)\), possible since primes are unbounded; because \(p\) is prime, the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)\le 2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), the proposed lower bound is \(\sqrt{\log p}>2\) since \(p\ge55>e^4\), giving a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
We disprove the proposed eventual lower bound by taking
\(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). In fact, there are arbitrarily large values of \(n\) for which \(a(n)=2\), whereas \((\log n)^{1/2}\) is eventually larger than \(2\).

First consider a prime number \(p\). We claim that
\[
a(p)=2.
\]
Certainly both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted. The integer \(1\) has no prime factors, so its set of prime factors is a subset of every set. The prime factors of \(p\) form the singleton set \(\{p\}\), so \(p\) is also counted.

Conversely, suppose that \(k\) is counted by \(a(p)\). Thus
\[
1\le k\le p
\]
and every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to the singleton set \(\{p\}\). There are two cases. If \(k=1\), it is one of the two integers already identified. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Since \(k\) is counted, \(q\) must be a prime factor of \(p\); because \(p\) is prime, this forces \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\). But a positive multiple of \(p\) that is at most \(p\) must equal \(p\). Therefore every counted \(k\) is either \(1\) or \(p\), proving the claim.

We will also use the explicit estimate
\[
e^4<55.
\]
For completeness, this can be obtained from the exponential series. We have
\[
e=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}.
\]
The sum through \(j=6\) is
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{6}\frac1{j!}=\frac{1957}{720}.
\]
For \(r\ge0\),
\[
(7+r)!=7!\,(8\cdot9\cdots(7+r))\ge 7!\,8^r,
\]
where for \(r=0\) the product is empty. Consequently the remaining tail satisfies
\[
\sum_{j=7}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
\le \frac1{7!}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac1{8^r}
=\frac1{5040}\cdot\frac87
=\frac1{4410}.
\]
It follows that
\[
e\le \frac{1957}{720}+\frac1{4410}
=\frac{31967}{11760}
<\frac{68}{25}=2.72.
\]
(The final difference is \(\frac{101}{58800}>0\).) Hence
\[
e^4<\left(\frac{68}{25}\right)^4
=\frac{21381376}{390625}
<55,
\]
with the last inequality following, for example, because
\[
55-\frac{21381376}{390625}=\frac{102999}{390625}>0.
\]
Thus, since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive reals,
\[
4=\log(e^4)<\log 55.
\]
In particular, whenever \(p\ge55\),
\[
\log p\ge\log55>4.
\]
Taking square roots, which preserves strict inequalities between nonnegative numbers, gives
\[
\sqrt{\log p}>\sqrt4=2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>2.
\]

Now suppose, toward a contradiction, that the conjectured assertion were true: for every \(\epsilon>0\), there were an integer \(N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
a(n)\ge (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}.
\]
Apply this assertion with \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). We would obtain an integer \(N\) such that
\[
a(n)\ge (\log n)^{1/2}
\]
for every \(n\ge N\).

There are primes larger than every prescribed bound, so choose a prime
\[
p\ge \max\{N,55\}.
\]
Since \(p\ge N\), the alleged lower bound applies to \(p\), giving
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
The classification at prime indices gives \(a(p)=2\), while \(p\ge55\) gives
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]
Combining these inequalities yields
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2,
\]
an impossibility.

Therefore, already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold \(N\) can make the proposed inequality hold for every \(n\ge N\). Hence the conjecture
\[
\forall\epsilon>0,\quad a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n
\]
is false.
